settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: No confirmation that any external attacker can supply the archive in a deployed usage; the repository only exposes library APIs plus test/example callers.
Entry data is written from the archive's decompressed stream; the primary impact path (overwrite outside destination) requires filesystem write permissions.
java.util.zip.ZipFile/ZipInputStream are used to read entries; the entry name is taken from the central directory, but this does not add traversal protection.
candidates.description: The extraction callbacks build destination paths by concatenating the output directory with the raw archive entry name and then write/copy file content there, with no traversal check. In ZipUtil.Unpacker.process the name is produced by mapper.map(zipEntry.getName()) and used as `new File(outputDir, name)` (ZipUtil.java lines 1150-1163); directories are created via FileUtils.forceMkdir and files via FileUtils.copy(in, file). ZipUtil.BackslashUnpacker.process does the same for backslash-separated names, splitting the entry name into path segments and creating each segment directory before copying the final segment (lines 1208-1226). ZipUtil.Unwraper.process also uses `new File(outputDir, name)` (lines 1258-1270), and Zips.UnpackingCallback.process uses `new File(destination, entryName)` and writes via FileUtils.copy / transformIntoFile (Zips.java lines 675-700). No normalization or containment check exists: searches for `normalize` and `..` in main sources returned no matches, and the `getCanonicalPath` match is only in the unrelated FileUtilsV2_2 copy routine. Therefore an entry named e.g. `../../etc/cron.d/job` (or a name that resolves outside outputDir) causes the extracted file to be created outside the intended directory, potentially overwriting arbitrary writable files. Note java.util.zip.ZipEntry does not itself reject `..` path segments; the value originates from the archive. This is a candidate: the library is API-driven and no in-repo caller/endpoint proving remote reachability was located.
missing_evidence: No application-level call site in this repository that passes attacker-controlled archives to unpack/unwrap (library-only code, examples/tests only).
No exploit execution or test was run to confirm a file is created outside outputDir.
Whether any consuming project relies on the output-directory guarantee is unknown.
Numeric line references are from the read source span; exact offsets may need re-verification.
preconditions: Application calls a ZipUtil.unpack/unwrap/Zips.unpack extraction API on an archive whose entry names originate from an untrusted source.
The process running the extraction has write permission to a path outside the chosen output directory (e.g. for overwrite of config/executable files).
No caller-supplied NameMapper strips traversal segments before extraction.
candidates.title: ZIP extraction writes entry names without path containment (Zip Slip / path traversal)

counter_evidence: The mode is masked with & 0777 before building permissions, which excludes setuid/setgid/sticky for the stored value in this code path.
Only used when the archive entry actually contains an AsiExtraField; otherwise permissions is null and no change occurs.
Java7Nio2ApiPermissionsStrategy / Java6FileApiPermissionsStrategy were not fully read to confirm exactly which bits are applied.
candidates.description: ZipEntryUtil.getZTFilePermissions reads the 'ASi Unix' extra field from each entry and returns a ZTFilePermissions object derived from the entry's mode bits (ZipEntryUtil.java lines 190-204 and 164-181, using AsiExtraField mode & 0777). During extraction, ZipUtil.Unpacker.process obtains these permissions and applies them to the created file/directory via ZTFilePermissionsUtil.getDefaultStategy().setPermissions(file, permissions) (ZipUtil.java lines 1166-1169). The permission value is fully attacker-controlled via the archive's extra field; there is no policy filter limiting which mode bits are applied (e.g. setuid/setgid/sticky bits are read as mode & 0777, so they appear masked out, but arbitrary read/write/execute combinations across user/group/other are honored). Depending on the underlying strategy, privileged bits and overly permissive modes on extracted files could weaken the security posture of the extraction target. This is a candidate only; I did not confirm the exact bits set by each strategy.
missing_evidence: Not confirmed exactly which permission bits each strategy sets (files not fully inspected).
No evidence that this leads to privilege escalation in a specific deployment.
No confirmed attacker scenario in this repository.
preconditions: Application extracts an untrusted archive that carries an 'ASi Unix' extra field with chosen mode bits.
The permission-setting strategy is available and applied on the target OS (POSIX), affecting the resulting file modes.
candidates.title: Extraction applies archive-supplied POSIX permissions to created files/directories
